validated_results.title: Are retinol, vitamin C, vitamin E, folate and carotenoids intake associated with bladder cancer risk? Results from the Netherlands Cohort Study.
validated_results.reason: Prospective case-cohort analysis within the Netherlands Cohort Study reporting dietary vitamin C intake and incident bladder cancer risk with a quantitative relative risk.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quintile of dietary vitamin C intake
extraction.population: Adults aged 55-69 years at baseline in the Netherlands Cohort Study

sample_size.excerpt: After 6.3 years of follow-up, data from 569 cases and 3123 subcohort members were available for case-cohort analyses.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 569 + 3123 = 3692

cases.excerpt: After 6.3 years of follow-up, data from 569 cases and 3123 subcohort members were available for case-cohort analyses.

effect_size.excerpt: Only vitamin C (RR: 0.81, 95% CI: 0.61-1.07, P-trend = 0.08), and b-cryptoxanthin intake (RR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.53-1.03, P-trend < 0.01) were inversely associated with bladder cancer risk.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Only vitamin C (RR: 0.81, 95% CI: 0.61-1.07, P-trend = 0.08), and b-cryptoxanthin intake (RR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.53-1.03, P-trend < 0.01) were inversely associated with bladder cancer risk.

comparison.excerpt: comparing highest to lowest quintile of intake

design.excerpt: In the Netherlands Cohort Study among 120 852 subjects aged 55-69 years at baseline (1986)

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Exposure status was measured with a food-frequency questionnaire.

gender.excerpt: The age-, sex-, and smoking-adjusted relative risks (RRs)

extraction.p_value_method: two-sided Wald test from effect and 95% CI on the log scale
extraction.ethnicity_basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available

validated_results.title: Are retinol, vitamin C, vitamin E, folate and carotenoids intake associated with bladder cancer risk? Results from the Netherlands Cohort Study.
validated_results.reason: Same prospective cohort reports a smoking-adjusted relative risk for dietary vitamin E intake and incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quintile of dietary vitamin E intake
extraction.population: Adults aged 55-69 years at baseline in the Netherlands Cohort Study

sample_size.excerpt: After 6.3 years of follow-up, data from 569 cases and 3123 subcohort members were available for case-cohort analyses.

cases.excerpt: After 6.3 years of follow-up, data from 569 cases and 3123 subcohort members were available for case-cohort analyses.

effect_size.excerpt: The age-, sex-, and smoking-adjusted relative risks (RRs) for retinol, vitamin E, folate, a-carotene, b-carotene, lutein and zeaxanthin, and lycopene were 1.04, 0.98, 1.03, 0.99, 1.16, 1.11, and 1.08, respectively, comparing highest to lowest quintile of intake. Only vitamin C (RR: 0.81, 95% CI: 0.61-1.07, P-trend = 0.08), and b-cryptoxanthin intake (RR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.53-1.03, P-trend < 0.01) were inversely associated with bladder cancer risk.
